usage: Polite-neutral; the default call to get a server's attention from your seat, pitched up at the end
Adds 좀 to soften the summons when the room is noisy or staff look run off their feet
Could you look over here, please?
Fuller and gentler — good when you've waved once and been missed
Swap in 사장님 / 이모님 in a small family-run place to sound warm, not just transactional
examples: 여기요!
Excuse me!
The single word, pitched up at the end, is a complete and normal way to call a server — no full sentence needed
여기요, 주문할게요.
Excuse me, we'd like to order.
Chain it straight into your request so the server arrives already knowing why you called
A: 여기요, 물 좀 더 주시겠어요? / B: 네, 금방 갖다드릴게요.
A: Excuse me, could we get some more water? / B: Sure, I'll bring it right over.
여기요 opens, a polite -주시겠어요 request follows, and staff close with 갖다드리다 ('bring it for you')
nuance: 여기요 is literally 여기 ('here') + 요 (the politeness particle), so word-for-word it is 'over here, please' — you summon a server by calling out the PLACE rather than the person, which is exactly how Korean service-calling works and why it's fine to say before anyone has looked your way. It is polite-neutral: any customer can say it to any server, but it is NOT honorific, so to an elderly owner you'd warm it up to 사장님 / 이모님 or soften to 여기 좀 봐 주세요. The nearest rival is 저기요, a hair more tentative because 저기 ('over there') feels less pointed than 여기; Koreans swap them freely indoors, but 저기요 also works to stop a stranger on the street, whereas 여기요 is almost purely for service settings where you're already seated. The trap for English speakers is reaching for 실례합니다 as 'excuse me' — but 실례합니다 apologizes or asks to squeeze past, so calling a waiter that way sounds oddly stiff and over-apologetic. Raising your hand or even calling out across a busy room while saying 여기요 is completely normal and not rude in Korea; many casual places even have a call button (호출벨) you press instead.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word 여기 ('here') + 요 = 'over here, please', but as a set call it just means 'excuse me, server!'. The logic is that you flag the location, not the person — so it works even before you make eye contact, unlike English 'excuse me' which usually waits for a glance. That's why you can shout it across a room and still sound normal.

Polite-neutral and made for service settings: a customer to any waiter, fine in any eatery from a pojangmacha to a mid-range restaurant. It is NOT honorific, so to an older owner soften it with 사장님 / 이모님 or 여기 좀 봐 주세요. Raising a hand or calling across the room is expected here, not rude — and many casual spots have a 호출벨 (call button) on the table instead.

Nearest is 저기요, slightly softer because 저기 ('over there') is less pointed than 여기. Indoors they're interchangeable, but 저기요 also stops a stranger outside, while 여기요 stays in seated service. In a fancy restaurant with dedicated table service, many people skip both and just catch the server's eye or raise a hand — calling out can feel a touch loud there.

Softer/warmer ladder: 여기요 → 여기 좀요 → 여기 좀 봐 주세요 → 사장님, 여기요. Drop to bare 여기 only as 반말 with a server you actually know. You normally chain it with your request — 여기요, 주문할게요 / 여기요, 물 좀요 / 여기요, 계산할게요 — rather than leaving it hanging in the air.

Don't translate 'excuse me' as 실례합니다 here — that's for apologizing or passing by, and aimed at a waiter it sounds weirdly formal and apologetic. Also don't attach a name particle (여기요 씨); 여기요 addresses the situation, not a person, so 씨 has nothing to grab onto. And don't whisper it timidly — under-projecting just gets you missed in a busy room.

mistakes: Saying 실례합니다 to call a waiter.

실례합니다 means 'pardon me (for the intrusion)' and is used to apologize or pass by, not to summon staff. It makes a simple service call sound stiff and oddly apologetic, as if you've done something wrong. To get a server's attention, say 여기요 or 저기요.
Adding 씨 or a name and saying 여기요 씨.

여기요 flags the situation, not a person, so there's no name for 씨 to attach to and the result is ungrammatical. If you want warmth in a small shop, address the person directly with 사장님 or 이모님, not 여기요 씨.
Dropping to bare 여기 with an unfamiliar server.
Bare 여기 is 반말 and can land as abrupt or bossy to a stranger doing their job. Keep the 요 — 여기요 — unless the server is clearly a friend or it's an extremely casual stall where everyone is on 반말 anyway.

usage: Polite-neutral; flags a server or stops a stranger you don't know
Stacks 잠시만요 to briefly hold someone who's already moving past you
More formal lead-in when approaching a stranger or an elder carefully
Excuse me, do you happen to…
혹시 cushions whatever question follows so it feels less abrupt or pushy
examples: 저기요!
Excuse me!
Tossed toward a passing server so they turn and come over — a complete call on its own
저기요, 여기 주문 받아 주세요.
Excuse me, could you take our order here?
Use it to call staff over, then state what you need in the same breath
A: 저기요, 혹시 자리 있어요? / B: 지금은 만석이라 5분만 기다려 주세요.
A: Excuse me, do you happen to have a table? / B: We're full right now, so please wait about five minutes.
At the door; 혹시 softens the ask and staff reply with 만석 ('every seat taken')
nuance: 저기요 is 저기 ('over there') + 요, an attention-getter that literally gestures AWAY from the speaker, and that built-in indirectness is exactly why it feels softer and more tentative than 여기요 — Koreans reach for it constantly. It is polite-neutral and remarkably versatile: it calls a waiter, stops a stranger who dropped something, or opens a question to a clerk, which makes it the single most useful 'excuse me' to memorize first. The line against 여기요 is range and directness: 여기요 ('right here') is pointed and almost only for seated service, while 저기요 also works out in the world to address someone you've never met. To raise the formality with a stranger or an elder, shift up to 저, 실례지만… ('um, pardon me, but…'), which buys a softer entry into the conversation. The classic English-speaker error is parsing 저기요 as the literal 'that place over there' and getting lost — in this fixed interjection the location meaning is bleached out and it is purely 'excuse me'. Keep it standing alone; don't bolt a name or 씨 onto it, and don't use it to apologize, which is a separate job for 죄송합니다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 저기 ('over there') + 요 = 'that spot, please', but the spatial sense is bleached out and it just means 'excuse me'. Pointing 'over there' rather than at the person is what makes it feel deferential — you're not jabbing a finger at someone, you're gesturing into neutral space, which is also why it's gentler than the more pointed 여기요.

Polite-neutral and the most all-purpose attention-getter in the language: call a waiter, stop a stranger who dropped a glove, open a question to a clerk. Safe with people you don't know. With an elder or in a formal moment, upgrade the lead-in to 저, 실례지만… rather than relying on 저기요 alone, which can sound a touch casual for that weight.

Against 여기요: 여기요 is pointed and stays in seated service, while 저기요 also works outdoors on strangers. Against 실례합니다: 실례합니다 apologizes or asks to pass, 저기요 just summons attention — they are NOT swappable even though both render English 'excuse me'. Against 저 (a bare hesitation 'um'): 저기요 is a real call, 저 alone just stalls before you speak.

Casual-to-careful ladder: 저기 (반말, 'hey') → 저기요 → 저, 실례지만… (formal). Common pairings cushion the next move: 저기요, 잠시만요 (to hold someone mid-step), 저기요, 혹시… (to soften a question), 저기요, 뭐 좀 여쭤볼게요 (to ask directions). Drop to bare 저기 only with friends or as a hesitation filler before speaking.

Don't read it as 'over there' mid-conversation — as an interjection to a person it means 'excuse me'. And don't use it to APOLOGIZE for bumping someone; that's 죄송합니다 / 실례합니다. 저기요 only opens contact, it never says sorry — say it after stepping on a foot and you'll sound like you want to start chatting, not apologize.

mistakes: Reading 저기요 literally as 'over there'.

As a set interjection it just means 'excuse me'; the spatial meaning has worn off. 저기 있어요 ('it's over there') is the live spatial use, but 저기요 aimed at a person is a polite call, not a direction — don't go looking where they 'pointed'.
Using 저기요 to apologize for bumping someone.

저기요 only gets attention; it carries no apology. If you stepped on someone's foot or jostled them, you need 죄송합니다 (or 실례합니다), because 저기요 would sound like you're now trying to start a conversation with them.
Dropping to bare 저기 with a stranger.
저기 alone is 반말 and lands like 'hey' — too casual for someone you don't know. Keep 저기요 for politeness with strangers and staff; save 저기 for friends or as a 'um…' filler before you speak.

english: Could I have the menu, please?
usage: Could I have the menu, please?
Polite; the everyday customer line the moment you sit down
Could you bring the menu, please?
More polite/formal with -주시겠어요; names the physical 메뉴판 (board/booklet)
Let me see the menu again
When you want it back mid-meal to add an order
Could you recommend something off the menu?
Natural follow-on once you have it but can't decide
examples: 메뉴 좀 주세요.
The menu, please.
Said as you sit or the moment the server comes by — the plainest version
여기요, 메뉴판 좀 주세요.
Excuse me, could we get a menu?
여기요 to call, then ask for 메뉴판 (the physical booklet/board) you want placed in hand
A: 메뉴 좀 다시 주시겠어요? 더 시킬게요. / B: 네, 여기 있습니다.
A: Could we see the menu again? We'll order more. / B: Sure, here you go.
Asking it back to add dishes; staff hand it over with 여기 있습니다 ('here you are')
nuance: 메뉴 좀 주세요 is 메뉴 ('menu') + 좀 (softener) + 주세요 (the honorific 'please give'), the bread-and-butter way a customer asks for the menu. The 좀 here is NOT 'a little' — it is a politeness lubricant that turns a bare command into a gentle request, so dropping it (메뉴 주세요) is grammatical but noticeably blunter, closer to 'give me the menu.' Note the split between 메뉴 (the menu as concept/list, also the dishes themselves) and 메뉴판 (specifically the physical board or booklet); both fit here, with 메뉴판 clearer when you want the object placed in your hands. To go more deferential, swap 주세요 for 주시겠어요? ('would you give…?'), which reframes it as a question and reads as extra courteous to an older owner or in an upscale room. The English-speaker trap is over-translating 'can I get the menu' into 제가 받을 수 있어요? — Korean expresses 'can I have X' simply as 'please give X' with 주세요, since the 'can I' is already baked into the polite request. With family at the table you'd just drop to 메뉴 좀 줘; note too that many places now have QR-code menus, so you might instead ask QR로 보는 거예요? ('is it the QR-code one?').

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'menu / a bit / please give' — but the 좀 is not 'a bit/a little'. It's a softener that lubricates the request, so the real meaning is a polite 'could I have the menu?'. Without 좀 (메뉴 주세요) it's correct but reads as a flatter 'give me the menu.' If you truly meant a small amount of something, that's 조금만, a different word entirely.

Polite (해요체) and exactly right for a customer to staff in any normal eatery. Upgrade to 메뉴판 좀 주시겠어요? for an older owner or an upscale place; drop to 메뉴 좀 줘 only with family or friends at the table. You wouldn't say this to a peer about ordering — it's a server-facing request, always aimed at the person who can hand you the menu.

메뉴 vs 메뉴판: 메뉴 is the menu as a list / the dishes; 메뉴판 is the physical booklet or board. Both work to ask for it, but use 메뉴판 when you want the object in hand, and 메뉴 (not 메뉴판) when you mean the food choices, e.g. 메뉴 추천 ('a dish recommendation'). Saying 메뉴판 추천 sounds like you want the booklet itself recommended.

Politeness ladder: 메뉴 좀 줘 (반말) → 메뉴 좀 주세요 → 메뉴판 좀 주시겠어요? (most courteous). Situational spin-offs: 메뉴 좀 다시 주세요 (to reorder), 메뉴 추천 좀 해 주세요 (can't decide), 메뉴 다른 거 없어요? (asking for other options), 영어 메뉴 있어요? (asking for an English menu).

Don't render 'can I get the menu' as 메뉴를 받을 수 있어요? — that literally asks about your ability to receive and sounds strange. Korean wraps 'can I have' inside the polite 주세요, so 메뉴 좀 주세요 already means 'may I have the menu, please.' Likewise don't tack on 제가 ('I') — it's not needed and makes the request oddly self-focused.

mistakes: Translating 'Can I get the menu?' as 메뉴를 받을 수 있어요?

Korean doesn't phrase customer requests with 'can I get/receive'; it uses 'please give me' — 메뉴 좀 주세요. The literal 받을 수 있어요 asks whether you're physically able to receive the menu, which sounds odd and overly cautious to a server.
Dropping 좀 and saying only 메뉴 주세요 to staff.

It's understandable but blunt, closer to 'give me the menu' than 'could I have the menu.' The softener 좀 is what makes it polite and natural, so keep it: 메뉴 좀 주세요. The 좀 costs you nothing and instantly warms the request.
Using 메뉴판 when you mean the food choices.
메뉴판 is the physical menu board/booklet; the dishes/options are 메뉴. To ask 'what's good on the menu' say 메뉴 추천, not 메뉴판 추천 — the latter sounds like you want the booklet itself recommended to you.

usage: Polite; announces you're ready, to a server who's already there
Flags the server to COME and take it (a summons, not a declaration)
Formal 합쇼체 for stiffer, upscale, or business settings
What STAFF say to you; you reply with 주문할게요
examples: 주문할게요.
We're ready to order.
Said the moment the server arrives at your table — a simple heads-up that you've decided
여기요, 이제 주문할게요.
Excuse me, we'll order now.
이제 ('now') signals you've finished deciding and are ready to go
A: 주문 도와드릴까요? / B: 네, 주문할게요. 김치찌개 둘이요.
A: May I take your order? / B: Yes, we'll order — two kimchi stews, please.
Staff open with 도와드릴까요?; you answer 주문할게요, then list with the count + 이요
nuance: 주문할게요 is 주문하다 ('to order', from Sino-Korean 注文) in the -ㄹ게요 form, which announces YOUR OWN intention as a courteous heads-up: 'I'm going to order (now).' That -ㄹ게요 is the natural customer register — polite but unstuffy, and it quietly signals the action to the listener rather than ordering them around. The line against 주문 좀 받아 주세요 ('please take our order') is DIRECTION: 주문할게요 declares what you will do, while 받아 주세요 asks the server to do something (come and take it); use 주문할게요 when staff are already at your table, and 받아 주세요 to summon them over. For upscale or business meals you can elevate to 주문하겠습니다. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'I would like to order' and producing 주문하고 싶어요 — literally 'I want to order', which sounds like voicing a private desire rather than actually doing it; Koreans just say 주문할게요. Among friends the casual verb is 시키다 (뭐 시킬까? / 나 이거 시킬게), but to the server's face 주문하다 is cleaner and more respectful. Don't confuse 주문 ('an order of food/goods') with 명령 ('a command') — only 주문 belongs in a restaurant.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I will do an order' (주문하다 + the -ㄹ게요 'I'll' ending). The real force is a courteous heads-up: 'we're ready, I'm about to order.' -ㄹ게요 commits the speaker to an action while signaling it to the listener, which is why it sounds considerate rather than demanding — it's a promise about your own move, not an instruction to them.

Polite (해요체) and the everyday customer default in any normal restaurant. Drop to 주문할게 with friends deciding for the table; rise to 주문하겠습니다 (합쇼체) only in upscale or business settings, where 주문할게요 might feel a touch casual. Say it to staff who are present, not as an announcement to your own group across the table.

주문할게요 (you declare your action) vs 주문 좀 받아 주세요 (you ask staff to come take it) vs 주문 도와드릴까요? (what staff say to you). Direction is the dividing line: declare when they're present, summon when they're not, and recognize 도와드릴까요? as their cue to you. Against 시키다, that's the friend-to-friend verb, not the server-facing one.

Register ladder: 주문할게 (반말) → 주문할게요 → 주문하겠습니다 (formal). Among friends 시키다 is the casual verb (뭐 시킬까?, 시킬게), but to the server's face the cleaner choice is 주문하다. Extend it as 주문할게요, 잠깐만요 (need a second more), 추가 주문할게요 (ordering more), or 따로 주문할게요 (ordering separately).

Don't say 주문하고 싶어요 ('I want to order') to actually place an order — it states a wish instead of acting on it, and a server may keep waiting for you to start. Use 주문할게요. Also keep 주문 (a food/goods order) apart from 명령 (a command); only 주문 fits a restaurant, and 시키다 stays among friends.

mistakes: Saying 주문하고 싶어요 to order.

That literally means 'I want to order' and stalls at expressing a wish rather than doing the deed; a server may wait for you to actually start listing dishes. To place the order, announce it with the action form 주문할게요.
Using 시키다 as 시킬게요 to the server's face.

시키다 ('to order food / make someone do something') is fine among friends (뭐 시킬까?) but feels casual aimed at staff. To the server the cleaner, more respectful verb is 주문하다: 주문할게요. Save 시키다 for the table chat about what to get.
Over-formalizing every time with 주문하겠습니다.

합쇼체 can sound stiff or even stand-offish in a casual eatery, as if you're at a formal ceremony or a business meeting. Default to 주문할게요; reserve 주문하겠습니다 for upscale or business settings where that heightened register actually fits the room.

usage: Polite; while pointing at a menu item, photo, or dish in front of you
이걸로 = 'with this (choice)' — picking among options, very common at cafés
Add 하나 / 둘 / 세 개 to nail down the quantity
Chain 이거랑 이거 to point to two items in a row
examples: 이거 주세요.
This one, please.
Said while pointing at the menu or a photo of the dish — the bare point-and-order
저기요, 이거 하나랑 콜라 하나 주세요.
Excuse me, one of these and one cola, please.
Combine a pointed 이거 with a named item, each marked 하나
A: 이걸로 드릴까요? / B: 네, 이걸로 주세요.
A: Shall I get you this one? / B: Yes, I'll go with this one.
Staff confirm with 이걸로 드릴까요?; you lock the choice with the matching 이걸로 주세요
nuance: 이거 주세요 is 이거 (the spoken contraction of 이것, 'this thing') + 주세요 ('please give'), the point-and-order workhorse for any item you can indicate. Crucially 이거 ('this, near me') sits in a three-way set — 그거 ('that, near you'), 저거 ('that, away from both') — so you pick by where the thing actually is on the menu or table, and the wrong one leaves the server guessing. A subtle but important variant is 이걸로 주세요 (이거 + -로, 'with/by this'): use 이걸로 when you are CHOOSING among options ('I'll go with this'), and plain 이거 when you simply want the object itself; menus and cafés hear 이걸로 constantly. The English-speaker mistake is forcing the object particle in speech and saying 이것을 주세요 — natives contract to 이거 and usually drop the particle, so the full form sounds bookish at a table. Another is pointing 이거 at a person; 이거 is for things only, so you'd never indicate someone and say 이거 — that's rude. Add 하나/둘/세 개 for quantity (이거 둘 주세요), and note the close cousin 이거 뭐예요? only ASKS what something is, it doesn't order it.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'this thing, please give', i.e. 'I'll have this one.' There's no idiom hiding here — the work is done by the demonstrative. 이것 (written/formal) contracts to 이거 in speech, and the object particle 을 normally drops, so the natural spoken form is the short 이거 주세요, with the full 이것을 reserved for writing.

Polite (해요체) and standard customer-to-staff in any shop, stall, café, or restaurant where you can point. Drop to 이거 줘 with a friend or at a super-casual stall. It's a service request, not something you'd say to a peer about their own belongings — for that you'd use a different, more deferential frame entirely.

이거 주세요 (you want the object) vs 이걸로 주세요 (you're choosing among options — 'this one, then'). And mind the 이/그/저 trio: 이거 = near you, 그거 = near the listener, 저거 = far from both. Picking the wrong one points the server at the wrong dish. Against 이거 뭐예요?, that only asks 'what is this?', it never places the order.
Quantity: 이거 하나 / 둘 / 세 개 주세요. Listing: 이거랑 이거 주세요 / 이거 두 개랑 저거 하나요. Choosing: 이걸로 주세요 / 이걸로 할게요. Politeness floor: 이거 줘 (반말) → 이거 주세요. Pair it with a named item too: 이거 하나랑 콜라 하나 주세요.

Don't say 이것을 주세요 at a table — the full particle is bookish and stiff; speech wants 이거 주세요. And never point 이거 at a person (it's for things only); for a person you'd use a name, 저분, or 이쪽, not 이거. Also don't confuse it with the question 이거 뭐예요?, which only gets you an explanation, not the dish.

mistakes: Saying 이것을 주세요 in conversation.

The full 이것을 is bookish and the particle 을 is normally dropped in speech; spoken Korean contracts to 이거 주세요. The written form sounds stiff and overly careful at a casual table, like reading aloud from a textbook.
Using 이거 when the item is near the server or far away.

이거 is only for what's near YOU. If you're pointing at something across the room it's 저거; if it's near the listener it's 그거. The wrong demonstrative leaves the server guessing which dish you actually mean.
Confusing 이거 주세요 with 이거 뭐예요.
주세요 orders the item; 뭐예요 only asks what it is. If you want to buy it, say 이거 주세요 — 이거 뭐예요 ('what is this?') will just get you an explanation of the dish, not the dish itself on your table.

english: Could I get some water, please?
usage: Polite; the standard request in any eatery
Insert 더 ('more') for a refill of what you already had
More polite/formal with -주시겠어요, e.g. to an older owner
Many Korean places have 셀프 (self-serve) water; worth checking first
examples: 물 좀 주세요.
Some water, please.
Said to a passing server; the 좀 keeps it polite, not curt
여기요, 물 좀 주세요. 그리고 컵도요.
Excuse me, some water please. And cups too.
Chain a second request with 그리고 …도요 ('and … too')
A: 물 좀 더 주시겠어요? 다 마셨어요. / B: 네, 셀프바에 있어요. / A: 아, 감사합니다.
A: Could we get more water? We've run out. / B: Sure, it's at the self-serve bar. / A: Oh, thank you.
더 for a refill; staff may point you to the 셀프바 (self-serve station) instead of bringing it
nuance: 물 좀 주세요 is 물 ('water') + 좀 (politeness softener) + 주세요 ('please give'). In Korea drinking water is normally free and either self-serve or brought on request, so this is one of the most-used lines in any eatery — you'll say it constantly. Again 좀 is NOT 'a little' — it cushions the request; 물 주세요 without it is correct but curt. For a refill you slot in 더 ('more'): 물 좀 더 주세요, and without that 더 the server may think you've had none yet. To sound extra polite, especially to an older owner, phrase it as the question 물 좀 주시겠어요?. The English-speaker trap is asking 'can I have water' as a literal ability question — 물 마실 수 있어요? means 'am I able to drink water?', which probes permission or capacity rather than making a request; Koreans simply say 'please give water'. And since restaurant water is just 물, you rarely need to specify — don't over-explain with 수돗물 ('tap water') unless that's genuinely what you mean. Many places are 셀프, so be ready to be pointed to a water station (정수기) rather than served.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'water / a bit / please give', but the 좀 is a politeness softener, not the quantity 'a little'. The real meaning is 'could I have some water, please.' If you actually want a SMALL amount, you'd say 물 조금만 주세요, not rely on 좀 — the two are easy to mix up but do different jobs.

Polite (해요체), aimed at staff, and totally routine since drinking water is free almost everywhere in Korea. Upgrade to 물 좀 주시겠어요? for an older owner; drop to 물 좀 줘 with a friend at the table. Note many places are 셀프 — you may be pointed to a 정수기 (water dispenser) or 셀프바 rather than waited on.

물 좀 주세요 (first water) vs 물 좀 더 주세요 (a refill — the 더 is what marks 'more'). Without 더, staff may assume you have none yet and bring a first glass. Don't reach for 수돗물 ('tap water') as the default — restaurant drinking water is just 물; 수돗물 specifically flags the faucet, which sounds odd to request to drink.

Politeness ladder: 물 좀 줘 (반말) → 물 좀 주세요 → 물 좀 주시겠어요? (most courteous). Refill: 물 좀 더 주세요. Self-serve check: 물은 셀프예요? / 물 어디 있어요? / 정수기 어디 있어요?. Chain other requests: 물 좀 주세요, 컵도요 / 물 좀 주세요, 얼음은 빼고요 (no ice).

Don't ask 물 마실 수 있어요? to request water — that means 'am I able to drink water?' (permission/capacity), not 'please bring water.' The request frame in Korean is 'please give', so 물 좀 주세요, not a 'can I' ability question. Expecting bottled or paid water by default is also off — tap-quality drinking water is the free norm.

mistakes: Asking 물 마실 수 있어요? to request water.
That means 'am I able to drink water?' — a question about permission or ability, not an order. A server might just say yes and walk off without bringing anything. To actually get water, say 물 좀 주세요.
Saying 물 좀 주세요 expecting it to mean 'a little water'.

좀 is a softener, not a quantity word; it doesn't limit the amount, it just makes the request polite. If you truly want only a small amount, say 물 조금만 주세요 — that 조금만 is the word that actually caps the quantity.
Forgetting 더 when you want a refill.

물 좀 주세요 asks for water in general; for more of what you already had, add 더: 물 좀 더 주세요. Without 더 the server may think you haven't been given any yet and bring a fresh first glass instead of topping you up.

usage: Polite; hands the choice to staff when you can't decide
Asks for the popular pick — concrete info rather than their personal judgment
Asks for the house specialty specifically
examples: 추천 좀 해 주세요.
Could you recommend something?
Hand the choice to the server when you're genuinely unsure
여기 뭐가 맛있어요? 추천 좀 해 주세요.
What's good here? Could you recommend something?
Pair with 뭐가 맛있어요 to warmly invite their pick
A: 처음 왔는데 추천 좀 해 주시겠어요? / B: 그럼 제육볶음 어떠세요? 제일 인기 많아요.
A: It's our first time — could you recommend something? / B: How about the spicy pork stir-fry? It's our most popular.
처음 왔다 makes the ask natural; staff suggest with 어떠세요? + 인기 많다
nuance: 추천 좀 해 주세요 is 추천 ('recommendation', Sino-Korean 推薦) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The 해 주세요 (해 주다 = 'do as a favor') is what makes it a request for the server's help rather than a bare statement; the 좀 softens it further, so the whole thing reads as warm and trusting. It's the polite go-to when you can't decide and want the staff to pick for you — and asking it actually flatters their expertise. The nearest rivals are content questions — 뭐가 맛있어요? ('what's tasty?'), 뭐가 제일 잘 나가요? ('what sells best?') — which ask for specific info, whereas 추천 좀 해 주세요 invites them to choose for you; the dividing line is that the recommendation request leans on their judgment, while the questions fish for facts. The English-speaker error is using 추천하다 without 주다 and saying 추천하세요 — that commands the server TO recommend, like ordering them around, which is too blunt; the favor verb 해 주세요 keeps it courteous. Also note 추천 is a 하다-noun, so it needs the verb 하다: with the softener it's 추천 좀 해 주세요, joined it's 추천해 주세요 — but never 추천 주세요, since you can't 'give' a recommendation as if it were an object.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'recommendation / a bit / please do-for-me'. The meaning is 'please recommend something for me.' The key piece is 해 주다 ('do as a favor'): it converts the noun 추천 into an action done ON YOUR BEHALF, which is why it reads as a polite request rather than an order. Strip the 주다 and you'd be barking a command instead.

Polite (해요체) and a normal, even flattering, thing to ask staff — it trusts their expertise. Drop to 추천 좀 해 줘 with a friend; rise to 추천 좀 해 주시겠어요? for extra courtesy with an older owner. Pairs naturally with 처음 왔는데… ('it's our first time') as a lead-in that makes the ask feel earned.

추천 좀 해 주세요 (leans on their judgment) vs 뭐가 맛있어요? / 뭐가 제일 잘 나가요? (asks for facts — tasty / best-selling) vs 시그니처 메뉴가 뭐예요? (the house specialty). Use the recommendation form when you genuinely want them to decide for you; use the questions when you'd rather have concrete data and choose yourself.

With softener: 추천 좀 해 주세요; joined without it: 추천해 주세요. Politeness ladder: 추천 좀 해 줘 (반말) → 추천 좀 해 주세요 → 추천 좀 해 주시겠어요?. Narrow the scope: 메뉴 추천 좀 해 주세요, 안 매운 거로 추천 좀 해 주세요, 둘이 먹을 거 추천 좀 해 주세요, 여기 처음인데 뭐가 괜찮아요?.

Two traps: 추천하세요 commands the server to recommend (bossy, like an order) — use 추천 좀 해 주세요. And 추천 주세요 is broken because 추천 is a 하다-noun you can't 'give'; you must keep the verb 하다 plus the favor 주다. A third: 저를 추천해 주세요 means recommend ME to someone, like for a job — drop the personal object.

mistakes: Saying 추천하세요 to the server.

Bare 추천하세요 is an imperative ('you, recommend!') and lands as bossy, as if you're issuing an instruction to an employee. The polite favor form is 추천 좀 해 주세요, which asks them to do it for you as a kindness.
Saying 추천 주세요 without 하다.

추천 is a 하다-noun, so it can't be 'given' like an object — 추천 주세요 is ungrammatical. It needs the verb 하다 plus the favor 주다: 추천 좀 해 주세요 (or joined, 추천해 주세요). You do the recommending, you don't hand it over.
Over-literal 'recommend me' as 저를 추천해 주세요.

저를 추천해 주세요 means 'please recommend ME (to a third party)', as if for a job or an introduction. To get a food suggestion, drop the personal object: 추천 좀 해 주세요, or specify the domain with 메뉴 추천 좀 해 주세요.

english: Could you make it not spicy?
usage: Polite; asks the kitchen to remove the heat entirely
덜 ('less') when you want some heat, just not as much
Can it be made not spicy?
Checks first whether the kitchen can even do it
아이도 먹을 수 있게 해 주세요
Make it so a child can eat it too
Frames mild-ness around who's eating, a natural real-life cue
examples: 안 맵게 해 주세요.
Make it not spicy, please.
Said right after ordering a spicy dish — the plain request
저 매운 거 잘 못 먹어서 안 맵게 해 주세요.
I can't handle spicy well, so please make it not spicy.
Give a reason with 잘 못 먹다 ('not good at eating') so the ask lands softly
A: 떡볶이 덜 맵게 돼요? / B: 네, 가능해요. 어느 정도로 해 드릴까요? / A: 아이도 먹을 정도로요.
A: Can the tteokbokki be made less spicy? / B: Yes, we can. How mild would you like it? / A: Mild enough for a kid.
Check first with 돼요?; staff ask the degree with 어느 정도로?, you scope it by who's eating
nuance: 안 맵게 해 주세요 is 안 ('not') + 맵게 (the adverbial form of 맵다 'to be spicy', so 'spicily') + 해 주세요 ('please make it for me'). The -게 turns the adjective into a manner ('in a not-spicy way'), and 해 주다 asks the cook to make it that way as a favor — so literally 'please make it in a not-spicy manner.' You're describing HOW you want it cooked, not naming a separate mild dish. The key distinction is 안 맵게 ('not spicy at all') vs. 덜 맵게 ('less spicy'): use 덜 when you still want some heat, because many English speakers overshoot with 안 and end up with a flat, bland dish. 맵다 conjugates irregularly (맵다 → 매워요, but 맵게 for the adverb), and a frequent slip is 맵지 않게 — which is actually fine and natural, just longer; 안 맵게 is the crisp spoken default. Another trap is treating 맵다 like a verb and saying 안 매워 주세요 — you need the adverb 맵게 before 해 주세요, not the conjugated 매워. To check feasibility first, ask 안 맵게 돼요?, since some dishes are pre-made and can't be de-spiced.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'not / spicily / please make-for-me' = 'please make it in a not-spicy way.' The -게 builds a manner adverb ('not-spicily'), and 해 주다 is the favor 'do/make for me.' So you're describing HOW you want it cooked, not naming a separate mild dish on the menu — the heat is a setting, not a different item.

Polite (해요체) and a normal special request to kitchen staff right after ordering. Drop to 안 맵게 해 줘 with a friend cooking or at a casual stall. A reason makes it land better: 매운 거 잘 못 먹어서… ('since I can't handle spicy…'). Some dishes can't be de-spiced once prepped, so 안 맵게 돼요? first is courteous and saves disappointment.

안 맵게 (zero heat — can come out bland) vs 덜 맵게 (less heat, keeps flavor) vs 맵지 않게 (also natural, just wordier). For a child you might frame it as 아이도 먹을 수 있게. Pick 덜 맵게 if you actually want mild rather than plain — the difference between 'tone it down' and 'strip it out' matters a lot in Korean food.

맵다 → 매워요 (sentence) but 맵게 (adverb before 해 주세요). Degree ladder: 안 맵게 / 덜 맵게 / 조금만 맵게 / 보통 맛으로. Check-first form: 안 맵게 돼요? / 덜 맵게 돼요?. Politeness floor: 안 맵게 해 줘 (반말) → 안 맵게 해 주세요 → 안 맵게 해 주실 수 있어요?. Same frame for other tweaks: 안 짜게, 덜 달게, 양파 빼고.

Don't conjugate 맵다 as a verb: 안 매워 주세요 is wrong because 매워 isn't a manner adverb. You need 맵게 before 해 주세요. Also don't reflexively pick 안 (none) when you mean 'mild' — that over-corrects into bland; 덜 맵게 keeps some heat. And misplacing the 안 (맵게 안 해 주세요) negates the wrong verb.

mistakes: Saying 안 매워 주세요.

맵다 is an adjective, and before 해 주세요 you need its manner-adverb form 맵게, not the sentence-final 매워. 안 매워 주세요 doesn't parse as 'make it not spicy' — it's a broken stitch of two patterns. Correct: 안 맵게 해 주세요.
Using 안 맵게 when you actually want mild, not bland.

안 맵게 strips out the spice entirely, which can leave a dish flat and lifeless. If you just want the heat dialed down while keeping the flavor, say 덜 맵게 해 주세요 ('less spicy') — that's the difference between toning it down and gutting it.
Putting the negative on the wrong word: 맵게 안 해 주세요.

맵게 안 해 주세요 negates the whole 'make' action and sounds like 'don't make it spicily (at all)', which is odd and ambiguous. The natural placement negates the adjective directly: 안 맵게 해 주세요 — the 안 hugs 맵게, not 해.

english: Can I get this to go?
usage: Can I get it to go?
Polite-neutral; checks whether takeout is even possible
Once it's confirmed, this asks them to actually wrap it
싸 주다 for taking home what's left on the table
A one-word answer when staff ask 드시고 가세요, 포장이세요?
examples: 포장돼요?
Can I get this to go?
Asked before ordering, to confirm takeout is even possible here
여기서 먹을 거예요, 아니면 포장돼요?
Will you eat here, or — can I get it to go?
Contrast 먹다 (dine in) with 포장 (take out) in one question
A: 드시고 가세요, 포장이세요? / B: 포장이요. 이거 포장해 주세요.
A: For here or to go? / B: To go. Please pack this.
Staff ask with 드시고 가세요?; you answer 포장이요 then request 포장해 주세요
nuance: 포장돼요? is 포장 ('packaging/wrapping', Sino-Korean 包裝) + 되다 ('to be done/possible') in polite question form, literally 'is packing possible?' — i.e. 'can I get this to go?'. The 되다 means 'is it doable', which is why it probes feasibility; once the answer is yes, you switch to the request 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it'). Korean increasingly also uses the loanword 테이크아웃, especially in cafés, but 포장 is the all-purpose, native-feeling term for any food. The dividing line: 포장돼요? asks IF takeout is available, while 포장해 주세요 ASKS them to do it — don't merge them, or staff may just say 'yes' and wait. The English-speaker error is rendering 'to go' literally with 가지고 가다 in the wrong frame, e.g. 가지고 갈 수 있어요? ('can I take it and go?'), which sounds like asking permission to carry it off; the idiomatic ask is 포장돼요?. For leftovers specifically, Koreans say 싸 주세요 ('please wrap it up'), and watch that 포장 (you carry it out) isn't 배달 (delivery to your door) — asking 배달돼요? orders a completely different service.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'does packing get done?' (포장 'packaging' + 되다 'be possible/get done'). The real meaning is 'can I get this to go?' The -돼요 probes feasibility, which is why it's a yes/no FEASIBILITY question, not yet a request to actually wrap anything. The -되다 ('get done') frame is what flags it as 'is this offered?' rather than 'do it now.'

Polite-neutral and aimed at staff, fine at any counter, stall, or restaurant. Drop to 포장돼? with a friendly stall owner; soften to 포장 되나요? for a gentler tone. Often it's the answer to the staff's own 드시고 가세요, 포장이세요? — at a counter you can just reply 포장이요 and skip the question entirely.

포장돼요? (is takeout possible) vs 포장해 주세요 (do it) — feasibility vs request. 포장 (native-feeling, any food) vs 테이크아웃 (loanword, café-leaning, mostly drinks). And crucially 포장 (you carry it out yourself) vs 배달 (delivered to your door) — 배달돼요? orders a totally different service that may not even be offered in-store.

Feasibility: 포장돼요? / 포장 되나요? / 포장 가능해요?. Request: 이거 포장해 주세요 / 포장으로 주세요. Leftovers: 남은 거 싸 주세요 / 이거 포장돼요?. One-word reply to staff: 포장이요 (vs 여기서 먹을게요 for dine-in). Politeness floor: 포장돼? (반말) → 포장돼요?.

Don't translate 'to go' as 가지고 갈 수 있어요? — that asks permission to carry it off and sounds like you're worried it's not allowed. The idiomatic line is 포장돼요? (to check) or 포장해 주세요 (to request). Keep 포장 distinct from 배달 (delivery), and don't stop at 포장돼요? if you've already decided — follow with the request.

mistakes: Saying 포장돼요? when you've already decided and just want it packed.
포장돼요? only asks WHETHER takeout is possible, so staff may just answer 'yes' and stand there waiting. To actually request it once you know it's offered, say 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it').
Translating 'to go' as 가지고 갈 수 있어요?

That means 'am I allowed to carry it away?' and frames it as a permission question, which sounds unsure and slightly anxious. The natural takeout phrases are 포장돼요? (to check) and 포장해 주세요 (to request).
Confusing 포장 with 배달.

포장 is takeout you carry yourself; 배달 is delivery brought to your door by a rider. Asking 배달돼요? requests a different service entirely and many sit-down places don't offer it. Use 포장 for to-go that you pick up and carry out.

usage: Check, please / I'd like to pay
Polite; asks staff to ring up the bill
The version YOU say announcing your own action at the counter
Natural follow-on once you're at the register
What you ask AFTER paying — not the request to pay
examples: 계산해 주세요.
Check, please.
Said at the counter or to the server when you're ready to pay
저기요, 계산해 주세요. 얼마예요?
Excuse me, we'd like to pay. How much is it?
Pair with 얼마예요 to ask the total in the same breath
A: 다 드셨어요? / B: 네, 잘 먹었습니다. 계산할게요. / A: 32,000원입니다.
A: All finished? / B: Yes, it was great. I'll pay now. / A: That's 32,000 won.
다 드셨어요? prompts you; you close with 계산할게요 and staff state the total
nuance: 계산해 주세요 is 계산 ('calculation/reckoning', Sino-Korean 計算) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'), literally 'please do the reckoning' — the standard 'check, please.' Korean names the ACT of totting up the bill rather than a paper 'check', so nothing physical gets handed over; you're asking for the action. In Korea you usually pay at the front counter (계산대) on the way out, not at the table, so this is often said while standing to leave or handed to whoever's at the register — waiting for a check to arrive at your seat will leave you sitting indefinitely. The near-twin 계산할게요 ('I'll pay') is the version YOU say announcing your own action at the counter, while 계산해 주세요 asks staff to ring it up; both are common and natural. A casual stand-in is 얼마예요? ('how much?'), which doubles as 'let me pay' at the register. The English-speaker error is asking for 'the bill/check' as a physical object — 영수증 주세요 means 'give me the RECEIPT', which you get AFTER paying, not the request to pay; to settle up, say 계산해 주세요. Don't confuse 계산 ('the bill') with 영수증 ('receipt') or with the similar-sounding 계좌 ('bank account').

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please do the reckoning/calculation' (계산 'calculation' + 해 주다 'do for me'). It means 'the check, please / I'd like to pay.' Korean names the ACT of totting up the bill rather than the paper 'check', which is why there's no slip handed over — you're asking for the action of calculating and settling, not a document.

Polite (해요체), staff-facing, and usually said at the 계산대 (front counter) as you leave — Korean restaurants rarely bring a check to the table, so you go to the register rather than wait. Drop to 계산해 줘 with a friend treating; say 계산할게요 when announcing your own move at the counter.

계산해 주세요 (you ask staff to ring it up) vs 계산할게요 (you announce you're paying yourself). 얼마예요? doubles as 'let me pay' at the register. And keep 계산 ('the bill') apart from 영수증 ('receipt', handed AFTER) and 계좌 ('bank account', totally unrelated despite the similar sound).

Politeness ladder: 계산해 줘 (반말) → 계산해 주세요 → 계산 좀 부탁드려요 (extra polite). Self-announce: 계산할게요. Natural pairings at the register: 카드 돼요?, 얼마예요?, 따로 계산해 주세요 (split), 현금영수증 해 주세요 (cash receipt), 영수증 주세요 (after).

Don't ask for the 'check/bill' as an object via 영수증 주세요 — that's the RECEIPT, issued after you pay, so it won't make staff ring you up. To settle the bill, say 계산해 주세요. And don't expect a check delivered to your table; head to the counter, where payment usually happens in Korea.

mistakes: Saying 영수증 주세요 to ask for the check.

영수증 is the receipt you receive AFTER paying, so this asks for proof of a completed payment — it won't prompt staff to total your bill. To request the bill / to pay, say 계산해 주세요; the receipt comes later if you want it.
Expecting the bill to be brought to your table.

Korean restaurants usually have you pay at the front counter (계산대), not at your seat, so waiting for a check to be delivered can leave you sitting indefinitely. Say 계산해 주세요 as you head to the register.
Confusing 계산 with 계좌.

계산 is 'calculation / the bill'; 계좌 is a 'bank account'. They sound close but 계좌 has nothing to do with paying at a restaurant — 계좌 주세요 would bizarrely ask the cashier for an account number instead of letting you pay.

usage: Polite; each person pays for their own
1/n(분의 일) for an even per-head split of one total
The opposite — one combined bill (often one person treating)
I'll pay just for mine first
제 것만 to settle only your own portion ahead of the group
examples: 따로 계산해 주세요.
Separate checks, please.
Said at the counter when each person pays their own share
저희 따로 계산해 주세요. 제 것만 먼저요.
Please ring us up separately — just mine first.
제 것만 ('just mine') to pay only your portion ahead of the others
A: 같이 계산하세요, 따로 하세요? / B: 따로 계산해 주세요. / A: 네, 그럼 한 분씩 해 주세요.
A: Together or separate? / B: Separately, please. / A: Okay, one at a time then.
Answering the cashier's 같이/따로 question; staff line you up 한 분씩 ('one person at a time')
nuance: 따로 계산해 주세요 is 따로 ('separately, apart') + 계산해 주세요 ('please ring up'), used when each person in a group pays their own. The cashier will often ask 같이 계산하세요, 따로 하세요? ('together or separate?'), and this is your answer. Culturally Korea has long leaned toward one person treating (한턱 내다) or paying together (같이 계산), so splitting per item is less automatic than in the West — but 따로 계산 (separate) and 더치페이 (Dutch-pay) are now common among younger people, so it's a normal, unremarkable thing to ask for. The dividing line: 따로 계산 means each pays for what they had / their own check, while 같이 계산 (or 1/n, 'split into N') means one combined bill. The English-speaker error is saying 'split the bill' as 나눠 주세요 ('please divide it'), which is vague and can be mistaken for dividing the FOOD; the clear requests are 따로 계산해 주세요 (separate) or 1/n로 해 주세요 (even split). Keep the word order — 따로 modifies 계산, so lead with 따로 계산, since 계산 따로 sounds reshuffled. And don't assume separate is the default; if you want it, state it outright before the cashier rings up one total.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'separately / please ring up' (따로 'apart' + 계산해 주다). It means 'separate checks — each of us pays our own.' 따로 directly modifies 계산, so the natural order is 따로 계산해 주세요; 계산 따로 해 주세요 sounds reshuffled and non-native, like the words landed out of sequence.

Polite (해요체), said to the cashier at the 계산대. Drop to 따로 계산해 줘 among friends. Socially, be aware Korea often defaults to one person treating or paying together, so if you want to split you should state it outright — don't assume the cashier will offer separate checks the way a Western server might.

따로 계산 (each pays for their own items) vs 1/n로 (one total split evenly per head) vs 같이 계산 (one combined bill, often one person treats). 더치페이 is the casual umbrella term for splitting. Choose by HOW you want the money divided: by what each person actually ate, or evenly across heads regardless of who ordered what.

Emphatic: 따로따로 해 주세요 (stresses every single person separately). Even split: 1/n로 해 주세요 / 1/n로 나눠서 계산할게요. Partial: 제 것만 먼저 계산할게요. Opposite: 같이 계산할게요 / 제가 다 계산할게요 (I'll treat). Politeness floor: 따로 계산해 줘 (반말) → 따로 계산해 주세요.

Don't say 나눠 주세요 for 'split the bill' — 나누다 ('divide') is vague and can sound like splitting the FOOD into portions. Be specific: 따로 계산해 주세요 (separate checks) or 1/n로 해 주세요 (even split). And don't assume separate is the default — Korea often expects one payment, so say it explicitly up front.

mistakes: Saying 나눠 주세요 to mean 'split the bill'.

나누다 ('to divide') is vague at a register and can sound like you want the food itself portioned out. For separate checks say 따로 계산해 주세요; for an even money split say 1/n(분의 일)로 해 주세요 — those name exactly how to divide.
Assuming separate checks are the default.

Many Korean places expect a single payment, and culturally one person often treats or the group pays together. If you want to split, you must state 따로 계산해 주세요 explicitly, or the cashier will likely ring up one combined total and hand it to whoever's nearest.
Misordering as 계산 따로 해 주세요.
The natural adverb order puts 따로 right before the verb phrase it modifies: 따로 계산해 주세요. 계산 따로 is understandable but sounds reshuffled and non-native, as if the words got swapped. Lead with 따로.

english: Thank you for the meal (before eating)
usage: I'll eat well / thanks for the meal
Formal-polite, said BEFORE eating to the cook or host
Polite but softer, to someone close who's treating you
Warm variant stressing how much you'll enjoy it
The HOST's matching line back to you — the other half of the pair
examples: 잘 먹겠습니다!
Thanks for the food!
Said to the cook or host just before the first bite
엄마, 잘 먹겠습니다.
Mom, thanks for the meal.
To a parent who made or paid for the food — warm and routine at home
A: 많이 차렸으니까 맛있게 드세요. / B: 와, 감사합니다. 잘 먹겠습니다!
A: I made a lot, so enjoy! / B: Wow, thank you. I'll eat well!
The host says 맛있게 드세요; the eater answers 잘 먹겠습니다 — the classic pairing in action
nuance: 잘 먹겠습니다 is 잘 ('well') + 먹다 ('to eat') + -겠습니다 (a formal future/intention ending), literally 'I will eat well' — the set phrase Koreans say BEFORE eating to thank whoever cooked or is paying. It's the eating-time counterpart to a host's 맛있게 드세요 ('enjoy your meal'): the eater says 잘 먹겠습니다, the host says 드세요, and together they form a fixed call-and-response. The register is formal-polite (-습니다); soften to 잘 먹을게요 with someone close, or drop to 잘 먹을게 in 반말 with friends/family. The line against 잘 먹었습니다 is purely TENSE: 먹겠습니다 (future) before the meal, 먹었습니다 (past) after — swapping them is the single most common learner slip. The English-speaker error is staying silent (English has no pre-meal phrase) or saying 감사합니다 alone — 잘 먹겠습니다 is the expected, almost obligatory line when someone feeds or treats you, and skipping it can quietly read as ungrateful. Don't announce it over food you bought entirely for yourself with no host present; it needs a provider to be aimed at, otherwise it sounds odd.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I will eat (this) well' (잘 'well' + 먹다 + -겠습니다 future/intention). The real force is 'thank you for the meal' said in advance. The future -겠- is the whole point: you're thanking the provider for what you're ABOUT to eat, which is exactly why the past-tense version (잘 먹었습니다) belongs after the meal, not here.

Formal-polite (-습니다), aimed at whoever cooked or is paying — a parent, host, senior, or even restaurant staff who served you. Soften to 잘 먹을게요 with someone close, 잘 먹을게 in 반말 with friends/family. Saying it is socially expected at a shared or hosted meal; silence can quietly read as cold or entitled.

잘 먹겠습니다 (eater, before) pairs with 맛있게 드세요 (host, 'enjoy your meal') — two halves of one ritual. Against 잘 먹었습니다, the ONLY difference is tense — future before, past after. 맛있게 먹을게요 is a warmer, more personal variant for someone close that foregrounds your enjoyment.
Register ladder: 잘 먹을게 (반말) → 잘 먹을게요 → 잘 먹겠습니다 (most formal). Warmer: 맛있게 먹을게요 / 잘 먹겠습니다, 감사합니다. Acknowledge the treat: 사 주셔서 감사합니다, 잘 먹겠습니다 / 덕분에 잘 먹겠습니다 / 차려 주셔서 감사합니다, 잘 먹겠습니다.

Don't stay silent before eating just because English has no equivalent — when someone feeds or treats you, this phrase is basically expected. And don't swap in the past 잘 먹었습니다 before the meal; that's the after-meal line. A bare 감사합니다 alone feels incomplete here — the meal-specific phrase is what's wanted.

mistakes: Saying 잘 먹었습니다 before the meal.

먹었습니다 is past tense ('I ate well') — that's the after-meal line. Used before eating it sounds like you're thanking for food you haven't even touched yet. Before the first bite, use the future 잘 먹겠습니다.
Skipping it because English has no equivalent.

When someone cooks for or treats you, 잘 먹겠습니다 is socially expected, almost a ritual that opens the meal. Silence or a bare 감사합니다 can feel cold or even rude; say the set phrase before you start eating.
Saying it about food you bought just for yourself.

잘 먹겠습니다 is directed at a cook or host you're thanking. Eating your own solo lunch with no one treating, you wouldn't announce it to a stranger or to no one — it needs a provider to be aimed at, or it sounds out of place.

english: Thank you, the meal was great (after eating)
usage: Thanks, that was a great meal
Formal-polite, said AFTER eating to host, cook, or staff
Polite, the slightly softer everyday form
Warmer — praises the food while thanking
Thanks to you, it was a great meal
덕분에 ('thanks to you') when someone treated you
examples: 잘 먹었습니다!
Thanks, that was great!
Said to the host or even called out to the server on the way out
사장님, 잘 먹었습니다.
Thanks for the meal, boss.
Called out to the owner as you leave a restaurant — gracious and normal
A: 입맛에 맞으셨어요? / B: 네, 너무 맛있어서 덕분에 잘 먹었습니다.
A: Was it to your taste? / B: Yes, it was so good — thanks to you, a wonderful meal.
Host checks with 입맛에 맞다; you close warmly with 덕분에 + 잘 먹었습니다
nuance: 잘 먹었습니다 is 잘 ('well') + 먹다 + -었습니다 (formal past), literally 'I ate well' — the standard thank-you AFTER a meal, said to the cook, the host who paid, or even called out to restaurant staff as you leave. It pairs with the pre-meal 잘 먹겠습니다; the only difference is tense (past vs. future), and swapping them is the most common learner error. Register: -습니다 is formal-polite; everyday speech often uses 잘 먹었어요, and friends say 잘 먹었어. A warmer version adds praise: 맛있게 잘 먹었습니다. The line against a plain 감사합니다 ('thank you') is specificity — 잘 먹었습니다 thanks specifically FOR the food/meal, so after eating it's the precise phrase, while 감사합니다 is generic and feels like it's missing the food. The English-speaker error, again, is silence (no English habit of thanking after eating) or mistranslating it as 'I ate well' in a dietary sense; it's a courtesy formula, not a comment on nutrition or how much you ate. Calling it out to the server on your way out is normal and gracious in Korea, not over-familiar.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I ate well' (잘 'well' + 먹다 + -었습니다 past). As a set phrase it means 'thank you for the meal' — NOT a comment on eating healthily or eating a lot. The past tense marks that the meal is over, which is exactly what separates it from the pre-meal future form 잘 먹겠습니다.

Formal-polite (-습니다), said after eating to the cook, the host who paid, or restaurant staff as you walk out — calling 잘 먹었습니다 to the owner on the way out is normal and gracious, not too familiar. Soften to 잘 먹었어요 in everyday speech, 잘 먹었어 in 반말 with friends.

Against 잘 먹겠습니다, only the tense differs — past after, future before. Against plain 감사합니다, this is SPECIFIC (thanks for the food), so it's the precise after-meal line; 감사합니다 is generic and feels incomplete here. You can stack them for warmth: 잘 먹었습니다, 감사합니다.
Register ladder: 잘 먹었어 (반말) → 잘 먹었어요 → 잘 먹었습니다 (most formal). Warmer/with praise: 맛있게 잘 먹었습니다. Crediting the host: 덕분에 잘 먹었습니다 / 사 주셔서 잘 먹었습니다 / 잘 먹었습니다, 또 올게요 (to staff, 'we'll come again').

Don't read it as literal 'I ate well/healthily' — it's a fixed courtesy. Don't go silent after a meal someone provided just because English has no after-eating phrase. And don't use the future 잘 먹겠습니다 once you've finished; that's the before-meal line, and using it after sounds like you're starting over.

mistakes: Saying 잘 먹겠습니다 after finishing.
먹겠습니다 is future ('I will eat'), the line said before the meal. After eating it sounds like you're about to start a second round. Once you're done, use the past 잘 먹었습니다 to close the meal.
Reading it as a literal 'I ate well (healthily)'.

It's a set courtesy meaning 'thank you for the meal', not a remark on how nutritious the food was or how much you put away. Treat it as a fixed thank-you formula, the same way English 'thanks, that was lovely' isn't really about nutrition.
Using only 감사합니다 after someone feeds you.
감사합니다 is generic 'thank you' and misses the meal-specific courtesy that Koreans expect after eating. The precise, expected phrase is 잘 먹었습니다 — pair them if you like: 잘 먹었습니다, 감사합니다.

usage: Polite-neutral; checks whether refills are possible AND free
Once confirmed, this asks them to actually refill it
Could we get more side dishes?
반찬 refills are usually free; 좀 더 주세요 is the everyday way to ask
추가 = a paid add-on; asks the price when it's NOT a free refill
examples: 리필 돼요?
Can I get a refill?
Holding up an empty cup or side-dish plate so staff see what you mean
반찬 리필 돼요?
Can we get more side dishes?
반찬 ('banchan') refills are often free in Korea — worth asking
A: 여기 콜라 리필 돼요? / B: 음료는 리필은 안 되고 추가는 돼요. / A: 그럼 하나 추가할게요.
A: Are cola refills free here? / B: Drinks aren't refillable, but you can add one. / A: Then I'll add one.
Staff distinguish 리필 (free top-up) from 추가 (paid add-on); you switch to 추가할게요
nuance: 리필 돼요? is the loanword 리필 ('refill') + 되다 ('to be possible') in polite question form: 'is a refill possible?'. The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility — and crucially whether it's FREE — which matters because in Korea side dishes (반찬) are frequently refilled at no charge, while drinks may or may not be. Once you know it's possible, you ask 리필 좀 해 주세요 ('please refill it'). The dividing line against 추가 ('an additional order') is cost: 리필 implies topping up (often free, the same item), while 추가 (추가요 / 추가해 주세요) means ordering MORE as a paid add-on — mixing these can land you a surprise charge on the bill. The English-speaker error is using 'refill' as if Korean had a native verb and saying 다시 채워 주세요 ('please fill it again'), which is understandable but unidiomatic; 리필 돼요? is what people actually say. For free banchan specifically, 반찬 리필 돼요? or 반찬 좀 더 주세요 both work, and the latter sidesteps the refill question entirely.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'does a refill get done?' (English loan 리필 + 되다 'be possible/get done'). It means 'can I get a refill — and is it free?' The 되다 keeps it a FEASIBILITY question, so it asks whether refills are offered, not yet a command to pour more. The free-or-not subtext is baked in, since Korean refills aren't uniformly complimentary.

Polite-neutral and staff-facing, common in casual eateries, 분식집, and bar-style spots. Drop to 리필 돼? with a friendly server. Softer: 리필 되나요?. Often you ask it while lifting an empty cup or banchan plate so staff see exactly what you mean without a long explanation.

리필 (top up the SAME item, frequently free) vs 추가 (order MORE as a paid add-on). Cost is the dividing line. For free side dishes specifically, 반찬 좀 더 주세요 works without even invoking 리필. Asking the wrong one — 추가 when you wanted a free top-up — can mean an unexpected charge.
Feasibility: 리필 돼요? / 리필 되나요? / 리필 무료예요?. Request: 리필 좀 해 주세요. Banchan: 반찬 리필 돼요? / 반찬 좀 더 주세요. Paid add-on instead: 하나 추가할게요 / 추가하면 얼마예요?. Politeness floor: 리필 돼? (반말) → 리필 돼요?.

Don't say 다시 채워 주세요 ('fill it again') — it's understandable but not how Koreans phrase it; use the loanword 리필. And don't assume every refill is free: drinks often aren't, even where banchan is. If unsure, ask 리필 돼요? 무료예요? before assuming it's complimentary.

mistakes: Assuming 리필 is always free.

리필 is often free for banchan, but drinks frequently cost extra or aren't refillable at all. Assuming it's free can mean a surprise on the bill; if unsure, ask 리필 돼요? 무료예요?, or check whether it's actually 추가 (a paid add-on).
Confusing 리필 with 추가.

리필 means topping up the same item (often free); 추가 means ordering an additional paid portion. Say 리필 돼요? to top up for free, but 추가요 / 추가할게요 when you're knowingly ordering more and expect to pay for it.
Saying 다시 채워 주세요 for a refill.

It's grammatically understandable ('fill it again') but not idiomatic, and may sound oddly literal to staff, like you're narrating the act. Koreans use the loanword: 리필 돼요? to ask, 리필 좀 해 주세요 to request.

usage: Polite-neutral; asking staff for the toilet
Fuller form with the existence verb 있어요
A heads-up before you step away from the table — not a location question
Is there a code for the restroom?
Many Korean toilets need a 비밀번호 (door code)
examples: 여기 화장실 어디예요?
Where's the restroom here?
Asked to a server when you need to go — the plain location question
저기요, 화장실 어디예요? 안에 있어요?
Excuse me, where's the restroom? Is it inside?
안에 ('inside') vs. out in the shared building corridor
A: 여기 화장실 어디예요? / B: 매장 밖으로 나가서 왼쪽이요. 비밀번호는 1234요. / A: 아, 감사합니다.
A: Where's the restroom here? / B: Out of the shop and to the left. The code is 1234. / A: Oh, thank you.
Many Korean toilets are outside the unit and need a 비밀번호 (door code)
nuance: 여기 화장실 어디예요? is 여기 ('here') + 화장실 ('restroom', Sino-Korean 化粧室, lit. 'grooming room') + 어디 ('where') + 예요 (polite copula). 화장실 is the standard polite word for a toilet — never the crude, dated 변소, which sounds like 'outhouse.' The 여기 ('here') scopes the question to THIS establishment, useful because a Korean restroom may be inside, down the hall, or in a shared building corridor that needs a 비밀번호 (door code), so 'where is it' is a genuinely live question. A fuller variant is 화장실이 어디 있어요? ('where is the restroom located?'), using the existence verb 있다. The dividing line: 화장실 어디예요? asks LOCATION, while 화장실 좀 쓸게요 ('I'll use the restroom') ANNOUNCES you're going — a heads-up, not a where-question — so don't swap them. The English-speaker error is over-politely asking 'may I use the bathroom?' as 화장실 가도 돼요? to a server when you really need directions; in a public restaurant you don't need permission to go, you need the location, so ask 어디예요?. Also keep the copula fused: 어디예요, not the split 어디 이에요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'here / grooming-room / where / is-it' — 화장실 is Sino-Korean 化粧室 ('makeup/grooming room'), a polite euphemism for the toilet, the same way English softens it to 'restroom.' The phrase plainly means 'where's the restroom here?' The 여기 ties it to this specific shop, which matters because the toilet is often NOT inside the unit.

Polite-neutral and staff-facing; fine to ask any server or owner. Drop to 화장실 어디야? with a friend. Always use 화장실, the neutral polite term — 변소 is crude and dated. In a café or bar the answer often includes a door 비밀번호, so be ready to ask for it if they don't volunteer it.

화장실 어디예요? (asks location) vs 화장실이 어디 있어요? (same, fuller, with 있다) vs 화장실 좀 쓸게요 (announces you're going — a heads-up, not a question). 화장실 가도 돼요? asks PERMISSION, which you don't need in a public place. Pick by whether you want directions or are just stepping away from the table.
Location: 여기 화장실 어디예요? / 화장실이 어디 있어요? / 화장실 어느 쪽이에요?. Heads-up: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 / 화장실 좀 갔다 올게요. Door code: 화장실 비밀번호 있어요? / 비밀번호 몇 번이에요?. Politeness floor: 화장실 어디야? (반말) → 화장실 어디예요?.

Don't ask permission with 화장실 가도 돼요? when you just need directions — in a public restaurant nobody's gatekeeping the toilet, so it sounds oddly childlike, like asking a teacher; ask 어디예요?. Also keep the copula fused as 어디예요 (not the split 어디 이에요), and avoid the crude 변소.

mistakes: Using 변소 instead of 화장실.
변소 is crude and old-fashioned, closer to 'outhouse/latrine', and sounds jarring in a clean restaurant or café. The neutral polite word for a public toilet is 화장실: 여기 화장실 어디예요?
Asking 화장실 가도 돼요? when you want directions.
That asks permission ('may I go?'), not location, and in a public place there's no one whose permission you need, so it sounds off — almost childlike. To find it, ask where it is: 여기 화장실 어디예요?
Saying 어디 이에요 separately.
The copula fuses onto the noun: 어디 + 예요 → 어디예요. Writing or saying 어디 이에요 as two separate pieces is unnatural; the smooth, native form is 화장실 어디예요?

usage: What staff ask; you answer with a number + 명
Your reply: native number + 명 + 이요
The HONORIFIC version staff use to you (분 + 세요)
There are three of us — is there a table?
State your number with 인데, then ask about seating
examples: 몇 명이요? — 두 명이요.
How many? — Two.
The host asks; you answer with the count plus 명
저희 세 명인데 자리 있어요?
There are three of us — is there a table?
State your number, then ask for seating in one smooth move
A: 몇 분이세요? / B: 네 명이요. / A: 네, 이쪽으로 오세요.
A: How many in your party? / B: Four. / A: Sure, this way please.
Staff use honorific 분 about you; YOU reply with plain 명, then they lead with 이쪽으로
nuance: 몇 명이요? is 몇 ('how many') + 명 (the counter for people) + 이요 (polite particle), the question staff ask at the door — 'for how many?'. As a customer you mostly ANSWER it, with 숫자 + 명 + 이요: 한 명이요, 두 명이요, 세 명이요. The counter 명 is the plain word for counting people, while 분 is its honorific; staff politely ask 몇 분이세요? (분 + the honorific copula 세요), but YOU refer to your own group with the humble/plain 명, never elevating yourselves with 분. That asymmetry — they honor you, you don't honor yourselves — is the key learner point. Native Korean numbers go with 명 (한, 두, 세, 네…), not Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼) — a frequent slip that instantly marks a beginner. The dividing line against 몇 사람? is register: 명 is the standard counter, while 사람 ('person') used as a counter sounds blunter and less polite in service. The English-speaker error is answering with Sino-Korean numbers (이 명) or honorifically calling their own party 분 — both sound off. Just say 두 명이요, and note a bare number ('둘') without 명 sounds clipped.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'how-many people?' (몇 'how many' + 명 'person-counter' + 이요 polite particle). It means 'for how many in your party?' This is mostly a line you HEAR from staff and answer; your reply mirrors the frame as 숫자 + 명 + 이요 (두 명이요), reusing their own counter back at them.

From staff it's polite-neutral (몇 명이요?) or honorific (몇 분이세요?). Your answer stays plain — 두 명이요 — because you don't honor your own group. Among friends deciding who's coming it's 몇 명이야? (반말). A bare number ('둘') sounds abrupt to staff; keep the counter 명 and the 요.

명 (plain people-counter, what you use for yourselves) vs 분 (honorific, what staff use about you) — never flip these. Against 사람 as a counter, 명 is the standard polite choice; 몇 사람? sounds blunter and more casual. So staff: 몇 분이세요?; you: 두 명이요 — the asymmetry is the whole point.
Native numbers with 명: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명, 네 명, 다섯 명 (NOT 일/이/삼 명). Your answers: 두 명이요 / 저희 세 명이요 / 두 명인데 자리 있어요?. Staff variants you'll hear: 몇 명이세요?, 몇 분이세요?, 일행이 몇 분이세요? ('how many in your group?').

Two errors: using Sino-Korean numbers with 명 (이 명 instead of 두 명), and honoring your own party with 분 (우리 두 분이요). Counters take NATIVE numbers, and 분 is only for honoring others, never yourself. Just say 두 명이요 — plain counter, native number.

mistakes: Counting your own party with the honorific 분.
분 honors OTHERS; for your own group you use the plain counter 명: 두 명이요. Saying 우리 두 분이요 wrongly elevates yourselves and sounds unintentionally self-important, like bowing to your own table.
Using Sino-Korean numbers with 명.
The counter 명 takes native Korean numbers — 한 명, 두 명, 세 명 — not 일 명, 이 명. So 'two people' is 두 명이요, never 이 명이요, which sounds like a beginner's miscount and stops the listener for a beat.
Answering 몇 명이요? with just a bare number.
A bare '둘' or '셋' can sound abrupt or incomplete to staff. Attach the counter and polite 요: 두 명이요. That's the natural, complete answer that mirrors the frame of the question they asked.

usage: Polite; flags a wrong dish gently with the soft -는데요 ender
주문하다 instead of 시키다 — a touch more formal
저희가 시킨 거 아닌 것 같은데요
I don't think this is what we ordered
Name what you DID order so staff can spot the mix-up
examples: 어, 이거 안 시켰는데요?
Oh, we didn't order this?
Gently flagging a dish that arrived by mistake, with a soft 어 in front
저기요, 이거 안 시켰는데요. 다른 테이블 거 아니에요?
Excuse me, we didn't order this — isn't it another table's?
Suggest the likely mix-up politely with 아니에요?
A: 김치찌개 나왔습니다. / B: 어, 저희는 된장찌개 시켰는데요. / A: 아, 죄송합니다. 바로 바꿔드릴게요.
A: Here's the kimchi stew. / B: Oh, we ordered the doenjang stew. / A: Sorry, I'll swap it right away.
Name what you ordered; staff apologize and fix it with 바꿔드리다 ('swap it for you')
nuance: 이거 안 시켰는데요 is 이거 ('this') + 안 ('not') + 시켰- (past of 시키다 'to order') + -는데요, a soft sentence-ender that signals 'just so you know…' and invites the listener to respond. That -는데요 is the politeness engine: it raises the issue gently and leaves the sentence open-ended, so you're flagging a problem rather than accusing anyone — exactly the tone you want when correcting staff. 시키다 ('to order food / make someone do something') is the casual everyday verb here; the slightly more formal 주문하다 also works (이거 주문 안 했는데요). The dividing line against a blunt 이거 안 시켰어요 ('we didn't order this') is TONE — the -는데요 version is softer and less confrontational, which matters because a flat negative can land like blame. The English-speaker error is dropping -는데요 and stating that flat negative, or misjudging the 시키다 vs. 주문하다 register. Another trap: don't say 이거 틀렸어요 ('this is wrong/incorrect') — that's for wrong answers like a math problem, not a mis-delivered dish; for a mix-up, say you didn't order it, or name what you did. And watch the near-homophone 식히다 ('to cool down'), which would garble the sentence entirely.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'this / not / ordered / but-you-see' (시키다 'order' + the trailing -는데요). The real meaning is a soft 'um, we didn't actually order this…'. The -는데요 leaves the sentence gently open-ended, handing the floor to staff so it feels like flagging an issue, not blaming them for it.

Polite (해요체) with the cushioning -는데요, ideal for correcting staff without friction. Drop to 이거 안 시켰는데 with a friend. 시키다 is casual-everyday; 주문하다 is a notch more formal if you want it. A small 어, … or 혹시 in front softens it even further, signaling you're puzzled rather than annoyed.

이거 안 시켰는데요 (soft, invites a fix) vs 이거 안 시켰어요 (flat, can sound accusatory). Even gentler: 저희가 시킨 거 아닌 것 같은데요 ('I don't think this is ours'). And don't reach for 이거 틀렸어요 — 틀리다 is for wrong ANSWERS, not a misdelivered dish; the dish isn't 'incorrect', it's just not yours.
Verb swap: 안 시켰는데요 / 주문 안 했는데요. Soften with a hedge: 시킨 거 아닌 것 같은데요. Redirect by naming yours: 저희는 OO 시켰는데요. Suggest the cause: 다른 테이블 거 아니에요?. Politeness floor: 이거 안 시켰는데 (반말) → 이거 안 시켰는데요.

Dropping -는데요 to a flat 이거 안 시켰어요 can read as an accusation pointed at the server. And don't say 이거 틀렸어요 for a wrong dish — 틀리다 means 'be incorrect (like a wrong answer)', which doesn't fit a delivery mix-up. Say you didn't order it, or name what you did. Beware 식히다 ('cool down'), a near-twin of 시키다.

mistakes: Dropping -는데요 and saying flat 이거 안 시켰어요.

The bare negative can sound accusatory, as if you're blaming the server for the mistake. The soft ender -는데요 raises it gently — 이거 안 시켰는데요? — so staff can fix the mix-up without feeling cornered or accused.
Saying 이거 틀렸어요 for a wrong dish.

틀리다 means 'to be incorrect', the way a math answer is wrong; a misdelivered dish isn't 'wrong' in that sense, so it sounds odd and confusing. Say 이거 안 시켰는데요, or name what you actually ordered: 저희는 OO 시켰는데요.
Confusing 시키다 with 식히다.

시키다 is 'to order'; 식히다 is 'to cool (food) down'. 이거 식혔는데요 would bizarrely mean 'I cooled this down', not 'I didn't order this'. Use 시켰- (the past of 시키다) for ordering — the two verbs sound close but mean entirely different things.
